Detention, Retention, and Infiltration

Follow one storm through storage, controlled release, permanent pool, infiltration, evapotranspiration, treatment, and bypass pathways before judging a stormwater practice by its name.

STORMWATER AND WASTEWATER · UNITED STATES FEDERAL FRAME · ILLUSTRATIVE ROUTES · EDUCATIONAL USE
WORKING PREVIEW · PREVIEW 0.3

First learn what detention, retention, and infiltration mean. Then follow one storm through storage, soil, outlets, wastewater I&I, permits, maintenance, and lifecycle value.

StartTrace the storm

START HERE

What actually happens to rain after it lands, and why the name on the drawing is weaker evidence than most people assume.

Who this is for

Anyone who has to talk about, pay for, inspect, approve, explain, or answer for a stormwater asset without necessarily being the person who designed it. That includes operators, inspectors, engineers working outside their specialty, asset managers, finance staff, executives, elected officials, developers, regulators, educators, and members of the public. The only thing assumed is that you know rain runs off streets and roofs into drains.

Why it matters

A utility can approve an asset that does not do what its name implies, spend capital adding capacity when the real problem was a blocked outlet, carry and treat rainwater in a sanitary sewer for years without attributing the cost, or tell the public a pond prevents flooding and lose credibility during the storm that proves otherwise. None of those failures require anyone to be careless. They require only that people trust a familiar word instead of tracing the water.

What you need first

  • Basic awareness that stormwater runoff moves from land into drainage systems or receiving waters.

How long it takes

Eighteen to twenty five minutes, including the interactive checks.

What you will be able to do

  1. Trace the possible surface, subsurface, controlled-release, overflow, bypass, and unintended wastewater pathways associated with one storm.
  2. Distinguish detention, retention, and infiltration without presenting one regional naming convention as universal.
  3. Explain a permanent pool and the temporary storm storage above it without inferring performance from appearance.
  4. Read the basic inflow, storage, and delayed-outflow story in a qualitative hydrograph.
  5. Select evidence that addresses timing, volume, concentration, total load, site constraints, and maintenance condition.
  6. Explain how wet-weather infiltration and inflow consume capacity in a separate sanitary sewer.
  7. Connect permit responsibility, maintenance evidence, lifecycle funding, and public value.
  8. Complete the 11-question system conversation while making uncertainty visible.

What this does not cover: This brief will not size, design, model, permit, inspect, operate, or certify anything. It does not give you a drawdown time, an infiltration rate, a separation distance, a removal percentage, or a compliance determination. It uses United States federal and EPA authority only. State requirements are handled separately.

IN 30 SECONDS

Three related terms. Three different parts of the water story.

  1. Detention holds stormwater temporarily and releases it later.
  2. Retention must be tied to the source because it may describe retained runoff or a permanent pool.
  3. Infiltration means water enters soil or porous material, but the final destination still has to be traced.
01
What do detention, retention, and infiltration mean before we look at a stormwater system?
Start here: what the three terms mean

What do detention, retention, and infiltration mean before we look at a stormwater system?

Start here: what the three terms mean

This brief explains three different ways stormwater can be managed after rain reaches a roof, road, parking lot, lawn, or other developed surface. The terms are related, but they do not describe the same physical action.

Detention means holding stormwater temporarily and releasing it later. Retention is a broader and less consistent term. It may describe water kept from later surface discharge, or it may describe a pond that normally contains a permanent pool. Infiltration means water moves from the surface into soil or another porous layer. Entering the ground does not, by itself, prove where the water ultimately goes.

Detention

Stormwater is held for a period of time, then released through an outlet or another documented route. The storage is temporary.

CORE TERM

Retention

The word is used in more than one way. Always check whether it means retained runoff, a permanent pool, or another source-specific condition.

CORE TERM

Infiltration

Water crosses from the surface into soil or porous material. Its later route may include native soil, groundwater, an underdrain, evaporation, overflow, or another exit.

CORE TERM

Learn the system words before reading the diagrams

A stormwater system is easier to understand when you can name what enters, where it waits, and how it leaves. These are the words used throughout the brief.

Each one gives you a plain meaning, something concrete to picture, and what the word does not establish. That last part matters most. Almost every expensive misunderstanding in this subject comes from a word being asked to prove more than it can.

Stormwater runoff

Rain that does not soak in, evaporate, or stay where it fell, and instead flows across the ground toward somewhere lower.

For example: Water sheeting across a parking lot toward a grate in the corner.

What it does not tell you: How clean it is, where it ends up, or whether anything is managing it.

Storage

Space where water is allowed to collect and sit for a while instead of continuing downstream.

For example: The empty bowl of a grassy basin behind a shopping center that fills during a storm.

What it does not tell you: How much space is actually available today. Sediment and debris consume storage over time.

Outlet

The structure that controls how water leaves a storage practice under ordinary conditions.

For example: A concrete riser standing in a basin with a small hole near its base and a grate on top.

What it does not tell you: That it is clear. A blocked outlet changes everything downstream of it and is invisible from the road.

Outfall

The point where flow leaves a drainage or sewer system and enters another system or the environment.

For example: A pipe end in a creek bank.

What it does not tell you: What happened upstream. An outfall is the last visible link in a long chain.

Overflow

The route water uses when it rises higher than the ordinary outlet can handle.

For example: A broad low notch in the earthen bank of a pond, usually dry, mowed, and easy to mistake for landscaping.

What it does not tell you: That it has ever been used, or that it is sized for the storm you are worried about.

Bypass

Water that skips some or all of the intended storage or treatment path.

For example: Runoff sliding past a clogged inlet and continuing down the gutter instead of entering the practice it was meant to enter.

What it does not tell you: That anything is broken. Some bypass is designed and some is accidental, and the two look identical from a distance.

Permanent pool

The water a wet pond is designed to keep between storms.

For example: The normal water line you see on an ordinary dry day, with a ring of vegetation around it.

What it does not tell you: That the pond is full or that no storage remains. Storm storage is normally provided above the permanent pool.

Underdrain

A buried pipe or drainage layer that collects water after it has passed through soil or engineered media, and carries it away.

For example: A perforated pipe in a stone bed under a rain garden, connected back to the storm drain.

What it does not tell you: Anything about recharge. If a practice has an underdrain, much of the water may return to the pipe network rather than reaching groundwater.

03
Why does a basin that looks empty still have value?
Dry detention uses empty space as temporary storage

Why does a basin that looks empty still have value?

Dry detention uses empty space as temporary storage

A dry detention basin is normally dry between storms. During rain, runoff enters faster than it leaves, so water temporarily occupies the basin. A planned outlet releases water while the water level falls and storage space becomes available again.

Read the five states from left to right. Compare the water level with the outlet in every state. The important idea is not that the basin looks empty after the storm. The important idea is that its empty volume is available to receive another event.

Find the detention function

The learner identifies temporary storage and later release without assuming a universal drawdown time or design performance.

LEARNING CHECK

Which observation best describes the detention function shown in the five-state basin sequence?

Return to the before, peak, and recovery states and identify what changes.

04
What is the permanent pool in a wet pond, and where does storm storage fit?
A wet pond can hold permanent water and temporary storm storage

What is the permanent pool in a wet pond, and where does storm storage fit?

A wet pond can hold permanent water and temporary storm storage

A wet pond normally contains water between storms. That normally wet volume is the permanent pool. When new runoff arrives, the water level may rise into temporary storm-storage space above the normal level, and water may leave through an outlet or a higher overflow route.

Begin at the pond bottom and move upward. Find the permanent pool, normal water level, temporary storage, ordinary outlet, and overflow elevation. The drawing explains their relationship. It does not provide transferable design elevations or prove treatment performance.

Read the permanent pool

Retrieval questions distinguish the normally wet pool from additional temporary storm storage above it.

RETRIEVAL CHECK

Distinguish normal pond water from temporary storm storage.

Read the pond cutaway from the normal water level downward, then upward.

05
What can the words detention, retention, and infiltration establish by themselves?
Names are clues, not proof

What can the words detention, retention, and infiltration establish by themselves?

Names are clues, not proof

EPA sources use detention consistently for temporary storage and later release, but retention is used in more than one way. One source may mean runoff kept from later surface discharge. Another may mean a permanent pool that remains while new runoff displaces water. The brief will state the intended usage and show the physical route every time.

Check the terminology boundary

The learner identifies which conclusion is supported when an asset is called a retention practice but no route, outlet, or objective has been documented.

LEARNING CHECK

An asset is called a retention basin, but you have no drawing, outlet information, or performance objective. What can the name establish by itself?

Recheck which answer preserves uncertainty without discarding the label as a useful clue.

06
After stormwater enters a soil or pavement system, where can it go?
Infiltration begins below the surface, but the route can still divide

After stormwater enters a soil or pavement system, where can it go?

Infiltration begins below the surface, but the route can still divide

Infiltration begins when water crosses from the surface into soil or another porous layer. Filtration is different. Filtration describes water passing through material that can strain, capture, or otherwise affect material carried with the water. A practice may involve both processes, but the words are not interchangeable.

Read the cutaway from the surface downward, then follow every side exit. Locate surface ponding, treatment media, native soil, the underdrain, seasonal groundwater, overflow, and receiving water. The drawing shows why disappearance from the surface does not prove recharge, treatment, or a safe groundwater relationship.

Three infiltration practices can divide water differently

A bioretention cell is a planted depression that receives runoff and routes it through surface storage, vegetation, soil, or engineered media. An infiltration trench is a stone-filled excavation that temporarily stores water while allowing movement into surrounding soil. Permeable pavement lets water pass through openings or porous material into a stone storage layer below the driving or walking surface.

These names describe common arrangements, not one guaranteed final destination. Compare the surface entry, storage layer, native soil, underdrain, overflow, and groundwater boundary for each practice. Ask which exits are actually present before claiming that water was recharged, treated, or removed from surface discharge.

07
What does a hydrograph show about inflow, storage, and outflow?
A hydrograph shows how flow changes through time

What does a hydrograph show about inflow, storage, and outflow?

A hydrograph shows how flow changes through time

A hydrograph is a graph with time along the horizontal axis and flow along the vertical axis. It lets you compare when runoff enters a system, when outflow reaches its highest rate, and how long flow continues after rainfall has slowed or stopped.

Read the curves from left to right. Compare the inflow peak with the later outflow peak, then look at the full area represented over time. A lower or later peak is not the same as a smaller total volume. The curves are qualitative teaching shapes, not calibrated model output.

08
Which evidence supports a flow, volume, concentration, or pollutant-load claim?
Stormwater performance has more than one measure

Which evidence supports a flow, volume, concentration, or pollutant-load claim?

Stormwater performance has more than one measure

Peak flow is the highest flow rate during the period being studied. Discharged volume is the total amount of water that leaves the defined system boundary. Concentration describes how much of a measured constituent is present in a given amount of water. Pollutant load combines concentration with the water volume moving across the boundary.

Compare these measures separately. A lower peak can help with one flooding or conveyance question. A lower concentration can help with one water-quality question. Neither result, by itself, proves a reduction in total discharged volume or total pollutant load.

Work through a basin that supposedly did not work

Definitions become useful when you reason with them. Follow this one all the way through before the next check.

Worked example

The situation: A utility receives complaints that a detention basin serving a commercial development is not working, because a creek downstream still rises after storms. The basin was inspected and found to be in reasonable condition. The outlet is clear. The basin filled during the storm and drained afterward, as intended.

Working it through: Ask what the basin was intended to change. Detention holds water and releases it later, so the total volume leaving the site over the full event stays close to the volume that entered. A basin with a surface outlet is a delay device, not a disposal device. If the complaint is that water still arrives in the creek, the basin was never going to prevent that. If the complaint is that the creek rises as fast and as high as it did before the development existed, that is a different claim, and answering it needs the inflow and outflow behavior, the contributing area, and whatever else drains to the same reach.

What you conclude: Not working is not yet a finding. The basin may be doing exactly what detention does while failing to deliver what the community was told it would deliver. Those are different problems. One is an asset problem and the other is an explanation problem, and the investigation and the fix are not the same in each case.

Where this stops: This reasoning identifies which question to ask. It does not establish whether this basin meets its design basis, whether that design basis was appropriate, or whether anything downstream requires a capital response. Those take site records, monitoring, and qualified engineering review.

Match the claim to the evidence

The learner matches flow peak, timing, discharged volume, concentration, and pollutant load to the evidence that can support each statement.

RELATIONSHIP CHECK

Match each performance statement to the evidence category that can support it.

Read the hydrograph and water-and-pollutant ledger again.

09
How can condition change the pathway the asset was intended to provide?
Condition can change the intended route

How can condition change the pathway the asset was intended to provide?

Condition can change the intended route

Maintenance matters because a stormwater practice depends on physical features that can clog, erode, settle, break, become overgrown, or lose access. Sediment at an inlet can reduce entry. Debris at an outlet can change release. Compacted or clogged media can change surface ponding. Erosion can create a shortcut that bypasses the intended route.

Start with what you can observe, then ask which water pathway the condition could affect. The trace separates observation, pathway question, possible consequence, and evidence needed. One observation is a reason to investigate. It is not enough to diagnose the cause or select a repair.

Separate observation from diagnosis

The learner moves from a visible condition to the pathway question and next evidence without issuing a diagnosis or repair instruction.

Change the condition, then trace the consequence

Connect a visible condition to the route it may affect, the consequence that may follow, and the evidence needed before diagnosis or action.

Model boundary: Qualitative authored cause chains for instruction. The interaction does not inspect, diagnose, rate, prescribe maintenance, or authorize work for a real asset.

10
How does stormwater or groundwater become infiltration and inflow in a sanitary sewer?
Infiltration and inflow put stormwater into the wastewater system

How does stormwater or groundwater become infiltration and inflow in a sanitary sewer?

Infiltration and inflow put stormwater into the wastewater system

In wastewater work, infiltration and inflow (I&I) describe unwanted water entering a sanitary sewer. Infiltration commonly refers to groundwater entering through cracks, defective joints, or other openings. Inflow commonly refers to rainwater entering more directly through connections, openings, drains, or similar routes.

Follow the intended stormwater route first. Then follow the unwanted wet-weather water into collection pipes, pump stations, storage, and treatment. In a separate sanitary sewer, this added water consumes capacity and requires pumping and treatment even though it should not have entered that system.

Classify infiltration and inflow

The learner classifies conceptual direct inflow and defect-related infiltration routes and then traces the capacity consequence without diagnosing a real collection system.

RELATIONSHIP CHECK

Match each conceptual wet-weather entry route to infiltration or inflow.

Trace each arrow from the rain or groundwater source to the sanitary sewer.

11
Why is a permit valuable after construction is complete?
A permit turns a public objective into assigned responsibility

Why is a permit valuable after construction is complete?

A permit turns a public objective into assigned responsibility

A permit is an authorization that places defined conditions, monitoring, reporting, and responsibility around an activity or discharge. In stormwater, the federal National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) framework connects public water-quality objectives to municipal, construction, or industrial responsibilities where the program applies.

Read the handoff from the public objective to the authorized condition, responsible party, funded work, records, and correction. The value appears when the physical system is maintained and the responsible organization can show what was done. This explanation does not determine whether a specific permit applies or whether a facility complies.

One storm writes into five ledgers

The same storm creates different questions across a utility. The water ledger asks where water went and when it left. The environmental ledger asks what reached the receiving water. The asset ledger asks whether storage, outlets, soil routes, and access still function. The financial ledger asks what service, maintenance, energy, renewal, or treatment cost changed. The public-accountability ledger asks who was responsible and what evidence supports the result.

Begin in the center with one physical event. Then move through all five ledgers. The purpose is to show that finance, engineering, operations, wastewater, leadership, and public communication should be connected to the same system record rather than built from separate assumptions.

Complete the responsibility chain

The learner orders responsibility, funded work, evidence, and correction and identifies a missing handoff.

RELATIONSHIP CHECK

Match each permit-to-value stage to the question it answers.

Return to the permit-to-value chain and identify the missing handoff.

12
What should each role ask about the same stormwater system?
Different roles, one system record

What should each role ask about the same stormwater system?

Different roles, one system record

Different professionals do not perform the same job, but they need a shared description of the system. An engineer may test assumptions and boundaries. An operator or inspector may report a field condition. A finance professional may ask what service and lifecycle cost are being funded. A wastewater manager may ask whether wet-weather water is entering the wrong pipe. A utility leader or elected official may ask what was promised, who is responsible, and what has been demonstrated.

Read each role question, then return to the shared record in the center. A useful record connects the water route, storm condition, storage, outlet, overflow, downstream boundary, maintenance condition, ownership, permits, monitoring, and budget. Shared terminology improves the conversation without assigning professional or legal responsibility to the wrong person.

13
Can I explain an unfamiliar stormwater system without overclaiming?
Explain the complete system without overclaiming

Can I explain an unfamiliar stormwater system without overclaiming?

Explain the complete system without overclaiming

Use the final conversation tool as a structured way to explain an unfamiliar stormwater system. Work from the physical system outward: identify the incoming water, normal condition, storm condition, storage, every exit, intended result, controlling features, responsibility, supporting evidence, possible failure route, and financial or wastewater consequence. Finish by stating one supported result, one uncertainty, one responsibility, and one next piece of evidence. Do not claim design adequacy, compliance, performance, or site suitability when the evidence does not support it.

Sources and scope

This working preview uses current United States federal law, federal regulation, and EPA guidance to explain a pathway-first method. EPA materials document that stormwater terminology varies and that performance can involve timing, volume, concentration, total load, groundwater protection, and maintenance.

This brief cannot determine a real asset's design, capacity, drawdown, infiltration rate, treatment performance, groundwater suitability, maintenance action, or compliance. Those decisions require current drawings, site evidence, approved procedures, applicable permits, and qualified judgment.

A USEFUL NEXT STEP

Take the outline. Build the procedure under control.

Copy this outline into the utility's approved workspace only after the actual asset, applicable authority, and responsible reviewers are identified. It is a review structure, not a maintenance or operating procedure.

Stormwater pathway review outline

  1. Asset identity and intended objectiveIdentify the exact asset, approved drawings, owner, design objective, drainage area, and the question this review must answer.
  2. Inflow and storm boundaryState what enters, the time period or storm condition being reviewed, and any upstream bypass or contributing area.
  3. Storage and treatment zonesIdentify each documented surface, media, soil, permanent-pool, and temporary-storage zone.
  4. Every exit routeList controlled outlets, underdrains, infiltration, evapotranspiration, seepage, overflow, bypass, and receiving-water routes.
  5. Site and groundwater evidenceIdentify soil, seasonal groundwater, contamination, pretreatment, well, karst, and nearby-use questions requiring qualified review.
  6. Condition and maintenance evidenceRecord inlet, outlet, sediment, debris, vegetation, erosion, ponding, underdrain, access, and post-storm observations without diagnosing from one observation.
  7. Performance evidenceState which evidence addresses timing, peak, volume, concentration, total load, treatment, and receiving-water response.
  8. Decision authority and follow-upName who reviews, what remains unknown, which approved procedure applies, and what evidence is required before any action.

WHERE THE BRIEF STOPS

A real SOP is a separate product.

A facility-specific SOP needs controlled inputs, applicable authority review, approved chemicals and equipment, named change authority, monitoring, rollback, safety review, version history, and approvals.

If OWOS builds that later, it should be an authenticated agent workflow. The agent would assemble evidence and route review. It would never invent settings or approve its own work.

What changed

What to observe
